blocks.x: CSM 177 · Computer Appreciation

Excel ships with hundreds of ready-made formulas — called functions — that replace long, error-prone manual arithmetic with a single, reliable instruction. This module covers how functions are built, where to find them, and the major function categories you will use throughout the course.

477+built-in functions shipped with Excel 2007, organised into categories 12+function categories, from Date & Time to Financial and Lookup & Reference 3classes of function by argument count — no-argument, fixed-argument, variable-argument
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define a function and explain why built-in functions are preferred over manually typed formulas.
2Describe the anatomy of a function — the equal sign, function name and arguments — and identify the three classes of functions by argument count, including optional arguments and placeholder commas.
3Insert functions using the Insert Function dialog and the AutoSum button, and name the 12+ function categories in Excel's Formulas tab.
4Apply Date & Time, Math & Trigonometric, and Statistical functions to solve everyday spreadsheet problems.
5Apply Text functions to clean, combine and reformat data held in cells.
6Apply Financial functions such as PMT, FV and PV, understanding the sign convention for cash flows.
7Apply Logical functions (IF, AND, OR, NOT) — including nested IF — and Lookup & Reference functions such as VLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Function A predefined, built-in formula supplied by Excel that performs a specific calculation using the values you provide. For example, =SUM(A1:A1000) instantly totals 1,000 cells — the alternative would be typing =A1+A2+A3+…+A1000 by hand.

Argument The value(s) a function needs to do its job, placed inside the parentheses that follow the function name. Arguments can be constants (typed numbers or text), cell references (e.g. A1, B2:B10), or nested functions (a function used as the argument of another function).

Optional argument An argument a function can run without. When an optional argument in the middle of the list is skipped, its placeholder comma must still be typed so Excel knows which argument comes next, e.g. PMT(rate, nper, pv, , type) — the empty slot before type marks the omitted fv.
Anatomy & Categories→ Date & Time→ Math & Statistical→ Text→ Financial→ Logical & Lookup
Building blocks
Every function shares the same basic shape. Learn that shape once, and every one of Excel's 477+ functions becomes readable.
Built-in functions vs. manual formulas

items: 1Fewer typographical errors — a single function call replaces dozens or hundreds of manually typed cell references and operators.
2Faster processing — Excel evaluates the built-in routine internally rather than you building the logic from scratch.
3Fewer keystrokes — compare typing =SUM(A1:A1000) to typing out 1,000 additions by hand.

blocks.x: Example — why PMT beats a manual loan formula Calculating a loan repayment by hand requires you to correctly combine the interest rate, number of periods, present value and future value into an amortisation formula. The PMT function needs only =PMT(rate, nper, pv, fv) — Excel supplies the amortisation mathematics internally.
Anatomy of a function
= (equal sign)→ Function name→ ( Arguments, separated by commas )

Reading =ROUND(A1, 2) The equal sign tells Excel a formula follows. ROUND is the function name. Inside the parentheses, A1 and 2 are its two arguments, separated by a comma — A1 is a cell reference, and 2 is a constant.
Three classes of functions, by argument count

c: Takes nothing inside the parentheses — the parentheses are still required, but left empty.
Always needs exactly the same number of arguments — never more, never fewer.
Accepts a range of possible argument counts — one value, several values, or several ranges.

blocks.x: Optional arguments, ranges & text

Placeholder commas for omitted optional arguments
Some fixed-position arguments are optional and can be skipped — but only if you keep their comma as a placeholder so Excel still lines up the arguments that follow. =PMT(rate, nper, pv, , type) omits fv (it defaults to 0) but keeps its comma so type is still read correctly.

Contiguous vs. non-contiguous ranges A range argument can be one block of adjacent cells (contiguous) or several separate blocks joined by commas (non-contiguous). =AVERAGE(A1:A25, B10:E15) averages two separate ranges in a single call.

Text arguments need quotation marks Any literal text passed as an argument must be wrapped in double quotes, e.g. =TEXT(A1,"dd/mm/yyyy"). If the text itself must contain a quotation mark, it is doubled so Excel doesn't mistake it for the closing quote, e.g. "She said ""hello""".
The Insert Function dialog & AutoSum

blocks.title: Using the Insert Function dialog (Formulas tab)

items: Click the Insert Function button (fx) on the Formulas tab, or in the formula bar.
Choose a category from the category list (or search by keyword).
Select the desired function from the list — a short description appears below it.
Excel opens the Function Arguments dialog, prompting for each required and optional argument with a live preview of the result.
Click OK to insert the completed function into the cell.

blocks.x: AutoSum button A one-click shortcut on the Home and Formulas tabs that automatically detects an adjacent column or row of numbers and inserts =SUM(…), e.g. =SUM(A1:A12). Clicking the small arrow beside AutoSum reveals a menu for Average, Count Numbers, Max and Min instead of Sum.

blocks.x: Date and Time category
Excel stores every date and time as a serial number — a count of days since a fixed starting point — which is what makes date arithmetic possible.
NOW() A no-argument function that returns the current date and time as a serial number, updating whenever the worksheet recalculates.
TODAY() A no-argument function that returns only the current date's serial number (no time portion).

DATE(year, month, day) — worked example =DATE(2010,9,28) returns the serial number 40450 — Excel's internal count of days for 28 September 2010. Any cell displaying this value can then be formatted to show it as a readable date.

blocks.x: Math and Trigonometric & Statistical categories
Two of Excel's largest categories — arithmetic and trigonometry on one side, data summarisation and probability on the other.

Radians vs. degrees Excel's trig functions (SIN, COS, TAN, etc.) expect angles in radians, not degrees. Use RADIANS(angle) to convert degrees to radians, and DEGREES(angle) to convert radians back to degrees, before or after calling a trig function.

blocks.x: Financial category
Financial functions calculate loan payments, investment growth and depreciation using a common set of time-value-of-money arguments.

Common financial arguments rate — the interest rate per period. nper — the total number of payment periods. pmt — the fixed payment made each period. pv — present value, the lump sum a series of payments is worth now. fv — future value, the cash balance after the last payment (defaults to 0). type — when payments are due: 0 for end of period (in arrears, the default) or 1 for start of period (in advance).

Sign convention Excel treats financial functions as flows of cash into and out of your pocket: negative values represent cash paid out (a loan payment, a deposit made), and positive values represent cash received (a loan taken out, a withdrawal). Mixing up the signs is the most common financial-function mistake.

blocks.x: PMT, FV and PV in practice

PMT — monthly loan repayment =PMT(12%/12, 60, -1000000.00) — a loan of 1,000,000 at 12% annual interest (1% per month), repaid over 60 monthly instalments, returns a monthly payment of approximately 22,244. Dividing the annual rate by 12 converts it to a monthly rate to match the monthly nper.

FV — savings goal =FV(10%/12, 15*12, -200000) — depositing 200,000 every month for 15 years (180 months) at 10% annual interest returns a future value of approximately 82.9 million. The payment is negative because it is cash paid out of your pocket into the savings plan.

PV — present value of an income stream =PV(5%/12, 60, 150000) — receiving 150,000 every month for 60 months, discounted at 5% annual interest, has a present value of approximately 7.95 million, shown as a negative figure because it is opposite in sign to the positive monthly receipts.
Logical & Lookup and reference categories
Logical functions make a spreadsheet decide; lookup functions make it search. Together they power payroll sheets, grading sheets and pricing tables.

blocks.x:
IF — overtime pay example
=IF(F1>40,(F1-40)*1.5,0) — if hours worked (F1) exceed 40, pay time-and-a-half on the hours over 40; otherwise there is no overtime pay.

Nested IF — discount tiers example
=IF(A1>=1000,0.15,IF(A1>=500,0.10,IF(A1>=100,0.05,0))) — an order (A1) of 1,000 or more earns a 15% discount; 500–999 earns 10%; 100–499 earns 5%; anything smaller earns no discount. Each nested IF only runs if the previous condition was FALSE.

blocks.title: Practice scenario — payroll with tax and levy deductions

blocks.x: A payroll sheet must compute an employee's net pay from: regular hours and an hourly rate; overtime hours (paid at 1.5× the hourly rate, using an IF test like the one above); then deduct Income Tax (15%), NHIL (2.5%) and District Assembly Tax (1%) from gross pay, and add a GetFund allowance for employees with more than 3 children (another IF test).

items: Store each rate (15%, 2.5%, 1%) once in its own cell, then reference it with an absolute reference (e.g. $H$1) in every row's formula — so the formula can be copied down the column without the rate cell shifting.
Gross pay = (regular hours × rate) + IF(overtime hours>0, overtime hours × rate × 1.5, 0).
Net pay = Gross pay − (Gross pay × $Income Tax$) − (Gross pay × $NHIL$) − (Gross pay × $District Tax$) + IF(children>3, GetFund amount, 0).
